claims.claim: A social movement is an organized, sustained effort by a group of people to create or resist social change. OpenStax's Introduction to Sociology 3e defines social movements as purposeful, organized groups that strive to work toward a common social goal; Encyclopaedia Britannica defines a social movement as a loosely organized but sustained campaign in support of a social goal, typically either the implementation or the prevention of a change in society's structure or values. Movements are collective — a single person's effort is not a movement — and they are not crowds: they last for months or years and need organizational and motivational mechanisms to sustain membership.

Sociologist David Aberle (1966) classified movements by what they want to change and how much change they want: reform movements seek to change something specific about the social structure; revolutionary movements seek to completely change every aspect of society; resistance movements seek to prevent or undo change to the social structure.

In the political-process framing of social movements — the tradition associated with theorists such as Charles Tilly and Doug McAdam — joining is explained by grievance (people feel a condition is unjust), identity (people see themselves as part of the group the cause speaks for), and opportunity (the political system looks open to challenge). A key premise of the framing is that grievances alone are not enough: movement formation requires all three factors, and political opportunities are what explain why movements rise at some times and not others.

Movements work by mobilizing, framing, and acting. Resource mobilization theory (McCarthy and Zald 1977) explains movement success in terms of the ability to acquire resources — primarily time and money — and to mobilize individuals; framing analysis (Snow and Benford 1988) holds that successful movements use diagnostic framing (stating the problem), prognostic framing (offering a solution), and motivational framing (the call to action).

Social movements have a life cycle. In the preliminary stage people become aware of an issue and leaders emerge; in the coalescence stage people join together and organize to publicize the issue and raise awareness; in the institutionalization stage the movement becomes an established organization, typically with paid staff; and in the decline stage people fall away, the movement successfully brings about the change it sought, or people no longer take the issue seriously (Blumer 1969 and Tilly 1978, four-stage process).

Movements have mixed results. OpenStax's account of the civil rights movement states that the movement in that period was an overall success and laws were changed, even if not attitudes, and that the movement continued and so did struggles to keep its gains; the decline stage of the life cycle can be a success, a failure, or a fading of attention. A movement may win policy change while attitudes lag, or win attention without winning policy.

Social change is the change in society created through social movements as well as external factors; collective behavior and social movements are two of the forces driving social change, and essentially any disruptive shift in the status quo, intentional or random, human-caused or natural, can lead to social change. General social change (technology, population, environment, modernization) is a sibling topic.

A movement is not merely a perpetuated crowd: a crowd does not possess the organizational and motivational mechanisms capable of sustaining membership through periods of inaction, and crowd mechanisms cannot coordinate activity over a wide area. When short-lived impulses give way to long-term aims and sustained association takes the place of situational groupings, the result is a social movement.

Political process theory (also called political opportunity theory) argues that the success or failure of social movements is affected primarily by political opportunities, with Doug McAdam, Sidney Tarrow, Peter Eisinger, and David Meyer among its prominent proponents; its three components of movement formation are insurgent consciousness (a collective sense of injustice), organizational strength (leadership and resources), and political opportunities (openings when the political system is vulnerable to challenge).

conflictingEvidence.issue: How much do social movements actually achieve?
positions: Some movements clearly win: OpenStax describes the civil rights movement as an overall success in which laws were changed — even if not attitudes (OpenStax 21.2).

Many movements fail or fade: the decline stage of the life cycle includes people falling away or the issue ceasing to be taken seriously, and political-process scholarship notes that movements can be derailed by social control, co-optation, and internal oligarchization (OpenStax 21.2; Wikipedia, political process theory).
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson states the honest note factually and without taking sides: movements have mixed results — some win, some fail, and many land in between, such as changing laws while attitudes lag. No real movement is evaluated or endorsed; the civil rights movement is used only as the textbook's own documented example of a mixed outcome.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Why do people join movements? Different theories emphasize different causes.
positions: Deprivation-style accounts emphasize grievances: people join because they feel deprived or mistreated (Britannica, which notes relative deprivation as a motive).
Resource mobilization emphasizes organization and resources (McCarthy and Zald 1977, via OpenStax 21.2).

The political-process framing holds that grievances alone are not enough — grievance, identity, and opportunity must combine, and political opportunity explains timing (Wikipedia, political process theory).
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents the three-factor account (grievance, identity, opportunity) and attributes it explicitly to the political-process framing, per the assignment, without depth or claims of consensus. Other theories are not disparaged; they simply are not taught here.
